scenario.title: What if ION Stage 2 went under Highway 401 and the Speed River? A 2.9 km twin-bore tunnel between Sportsworld and Preston
scenario.label: Illustrative scenario: not a Region plan
scenario.basis: The Region's 10-year capital forecast includes project 68030 "RT to Cambridge" (ION Stage 2): $85.0 million in 2027 and $2.05 billion over 10 years (2026 Budget Book, p. 43). The Region's approved Stage 2 route is mostly at street level. Between Sportsworld and Preston stations it must cross Highway 401 and the Speed River and its floodplain, and approach Preston's older core. This scenario asks what it would take to put that 2.9 km stretch underground instead, so engineers, staff and residents can weigh it. The Region has not proposed this, and the agents do not choose a site.

steps.title: Drill boreholes to read the ground
steps.plain: Crews drill about 49 boreholes: one every 75 m along the line, three at each shaft, and two on each side of Highway 401 and the Speed River. Each goes down past the bottom of the future tunnel by at least 1.5 tunnel widths, to learn what the soil, rock and groundwater are like. This decides whether a tunnel here is practical at all.
steps.whatResidentsNotice: A drill truck parked in a coned-off lane or on a boulevard for one to three days at each spot, daytime only. Some noise from the drill engine. Short lane closures on King Street East.

render.prompt: Scene: geotechnical investigation for a future light rail tunnel. A white truck-mounted drill rig with its mast raised drills a borehole in a coned-off lane of a wide suburban arterial road, with a concrete highway overpass and a multi-lane freeway in the background. A second small track-mounted drill rig works on the grassy boulevard. Two workers lay soil core samples in long wooden core boxes on a pickup tailgate. Orange traffic cones, a lane-closure arrow board trailer. Eye-level view from the sidewalk. steps.title: Fence the work sites and move utilities
steps.plain: The launch site (Surface parking off Heldmann Road by Moose Winooski's) and the extraction site (Industrial land off King Street by P&H Milling Group) are fenced with tall hoarding. Site offices, a wheel wash and a power supply go in. Pipes, cables and wires under the shaft footprints are moved out of the way first.
steps.whatResidentsNotice: Tall hoarding around the sites, lost parking, utility crews digging along nearby streets, and temporary lane shifts. Work mostly on weekdays, 7 am to 7 pm.

steps.title: Dig the launch shaft
steps.plain: A ring of interlocking concrete piles (secant piles) is drilled into the ground to hold back soil and water. Then the ground inside is dug out, about 22 m deep, with steel braces added as it goes down. Pumps lower the groundwater around the shaft and the water is treated before it is discharged. The smaller extraction shaft (about 22 m deep) is built the same way.
steps.whatResidentsNotice: The loudest stage on site: piling rigs and excavators in daytime, dump trucks leaving through the wheel wash, and pumps that may run day and night. Vibration is monitored at nearby buildings.

render.prompt: Scene: a deep rectangular launch shaft for a twin-bore light rail tunnel, about 24 m wide and 45 m long and 22 m deep, being excavated inside a fenced work site in a parking lot. The walls are a row of interlocking round concrete secant piles, braced by horizontal steel walers and big tubular steel struts across the shaft. An excavator works at the bottom, a long-reach clamshell bucket lifts soil out, dewatering pumps and a water treatment tank sit at the edge, dump trucks queue at the gate. Aerial three-quarter view looking down into the shaft. steps.title: Lower and launch the boring machines
steps.plain: Two tunnel boring machines, each about 6.5 m across and well over 100 m long with their trailing gear, arrive in pieces. Big cranes lower the cutterhead and shield into the shaft, where they are put together and pushed off a steel frame into the ground. Behind the cutterhead, the machine lines the tunnel with rings of precast concrete segments.
steps.whatResidentsNotice: Oversize loads on Highway 401 and Highway 8, usually at night with a police escort. One or two heavy crane lifts that may close a lane for a night. A gantry crane on site that works around the clock once boring starts.

Stacks of curved precast concrete tunnel lining segments wait in the yard. Elevated view from the edge of the shaft, late morning light. steps.title: Bore 2,828 m under Highway 401 and the Speed River
steps.plain: The two machines bore side by side, passing 13 to 27 m below the surface, deeper under Highway 401 and the Speed River. At about 12 m a day each, that is roughly 11 months of boring. They dig out about 187,683 m³ of soil, about 243,988 m³ once loosened: some 24,399 truckloads in all. Settlement is measured at the surface, on the highway and at buildings above the tunnels.
steps.duration: about 11 to 15 months (assumption: 12 m a day per machine)
steps.whatResidentsNotice: About 100 dump trucks a day (an estimate) leave the launch site while both machines run, about 9 an hour from 7 am to 7 pm, heading straight to Highway 8 and Highway 401. Boring itself goes on underground 24 hours a day and is rarely felt above. Spoil is stored on site overnight.

steps.title: Break through at Preston and link the bores
steps.plain: Each machine breaks through the wall of the extraction shaft and is lifted out in pieces. Between the two bores, 11 cross-passages are dug by hand-held equipment, no more than 244 m apart, so people can walk from one tunnel to the other in an emergency. Near the river the ground around a cross-passage may be frozen or grouted first to keep water out.
steps.whatResidentsNotice: Crane lifts at the extraction site to remove the machines, some at night. Ground-freezing plant may hum day and night for a few weeks. Little else shows above ground.

render.prompt: Scene: the breakthrough moment inside a deep rectangular concrete extraction shaft with straight vertical walls. steps.title: Fit out, then give the land back
steps.plain: Track, power, signals, ventilation and fire safety systems go in through the shafts. Each shaft becomes an emergency exit, a ventilation building or part of a station entrance. Then the hoarding comes down and the parking lots, streets and trees are put back.
steps.duration: about 12 to 18 months for fit-out and restoration (assumption)
steps.whatResidentsNotice: Fewer trucks. Deliveries of rail and equipment. At the end, new paving, landscaping and a small exit or vent building where each shaft was.

limits: Illustrative scenario only: the Region of Waterloo's approved ION Stage 2 route runs mostly at street level. Nobody has proposed this tunnel.

No geotechnical data: soil, rock and groundwater are unknown until boreholes are drilled. Glacial soils and high groundwater near the Speed River could change the method, the depth or whether a tunnel is practical at all.
No utilities data: buried pipes, cables and the Highway 401 bridge and culvert foundations are not mapped here.
No property data: the scout does not know who owns each site or whether it is for sale or lease. Sites come from OpenStreetMap tags, which can be out of date.
Distances are straight lines, not truck routes. Truck access is the distance to the nearest highway or main road.
Ground levels are from a national elevation model (CDEM, about 20 m cells, rounded to 1 m). The river bed is assumed 3 m below the water surface.

Durations, advance rate (12 m a day per machine), bulking (1.3) and truck size (10 m³) are typical assumptions, not a schedule. Cost is not estimated: tunnels usually cost several times more per kilometre than street-level track.

Near Preston the line follows the Speed River valley: the extraction shaft as placed would likely sit in the river's regulated floodplain, which could move it east, deepen the dewatering effort or change the method.
Stations: the scenario keeps Sportsworld and Preston stations where the Region placed them and does not design the portals or ramps that would connect the tunnel to them.
Renders are illustrative pictures made by an image model. They show the kind of work, not a design.
